newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups, industry against meat inspection fees.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups, industry against meat inspection fees.

text.p: A U.S. government proposal to shift most of the cost of federal meat inspection to industry faces stiff opposition from two unlikely allies: consumer groups and meat processors.
In its fiscal 1998 budget, the Clinton administration has proposed $390 million in user fees to cover the cost of putting federal inspectors in meat, poultry and egg plants.
Industry now pays unexpected overtime and holidays for meat inspectors. The proposal would require the companies to shoulder about 70 percent of the bill.

At a public meeting Monday held by the Agriculture Department, consumer groups said the user fees would undermine public confidence in meat inspection and put an unnecessary burden on an industry already implementing major reform.

"We oppose this effort very, very strongly," said Carol Tucker Foreman, former Agriculture Department assistant secretary for food safety during the Carter administration and head of a coalition of labour unions and consumer groups. "We think the ability of the system to adjust to this kind of change on top of change already out there is likely to bring the whole thing down."

Last year, the government announced an overhaul of the meat inspection process, introducing scientific testing for disease-causing bacteria to replace the so-called "sniff and poke" method. The system had not been updated since Upton Sinclair's expose on the Chicago stockyards, "The Jungle", led to enactment of the Federal Meat Inspection Act in 1907.

The Agriculture Department said budget constraints make it necessary for industry to chip in and that preliminary analysis suggested the effects would be "quite small." It calculates that if the whole cost of the fees was passed on to consumers, it would result in a $1.45 increase annually for each American.

Few industry officials attended Monday's session. Last week, 12 major meat associations sent a joint letter to the department calling the fees a "food tax" that would hurt both industry and consumers.

"At a time when the administration is calling for enhanced food safety protections, it seems highly inappropriate for the federal government to abandon its financial responsibility in ensuring the public health," the groups, which included the American Meat Instute and the National Broiler Council, said in the letter dated March 6.

The proposal must be approved by Congress and to go through the rule-making process before going into effect. Department officials said they expected a bill would to be sent to Capitol Hill in the next few days. Several key lawmakers have already indicated they are against the user fee proposal.
